https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9qr.text: Figure caption, Watch: Judge orders deadlocked Clancy jurors to keep deliberating By Ana Faguy reporting from court in Massachusetts Published 1 September 2026, 17:37 BST Updated 29 minutes ago Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying. Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023. Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong. After discussing the case for several more hours on Tuesday, jurors were sent home for the day and asked to return on Wednesday. "I just want to thank you for all your hard work and commitment so far in this case," the judge told jurors before sending them home. The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them. The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked. Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer. Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial Published 9 hours ago It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations. A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC. "If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Clancy in court on Tuesday But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said. Criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC she was not surprised to hear that the jury was deadlocked, as people had strong opinions on the case. "The facts are difficult and a lot of the evidence is graphic so they have a lot weighing on them," she said. The judge can declare a mistrial if the jury is not able to agree on a verdict. Image source, Plymouth Clerks Office Image caption, Clancy family picture exhibited in court Clancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home in January 2023. The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth, and that she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings. If found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person , Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole. She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars. If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed. She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life. https://aa.com.tr/en/world/openai-shuts-.text: World OpenAI shuts down Russia-linked ChatGPT accounts over ‘covert influence campaign’ Operators used AI to promote purported think tank, conceal Russian origins across social media platforms, according to OpenAI Mücahithan Avcıoğlu 25 August 2026 • Update : 25 August 2026 İSTANBUL OpenAI said Tuesday it shut down a cluster of ChatGPT accounts originating in Russia after uncovering a “covert influence campaign” that used artificial intelligence to promote a purported think tank and narratives favorable to Moscow. The US artificial intelligence company said the accounts generated social media content promoting the International Burke Institute (IBI), which described itself as an Israel-based “expert community.” The investigation began with AI-generated social media posts but uncovered a broader operation involving copied and misattributed academic studies, a purported “sovereignty” index that portrayed Russia favorably and efforts to conceal the operators’ Russian origins. The operators submitted prompts in Russian to produce mostly English-language comments that were later published on Substack, Telegram, X, Facebook and LinkedIn, according to the company. They also instructed ChatGPT to remove linguistic clues that could reveal they were Russian speakers. OpenAI said the operators used virtual private networks (VPNs) to access its services, as the company does not allow its models to be accessed from Russia. Much of the generated material promoted the IBI and articles on its website, which was registered in February 2025. A review by OpenAI found that 34 of a sample of 36 articles linked to purported experts on the website had been copied from elsewhere. Some were falsely attributed, while others appeared to have been machine-translated from a Slavic language. The organization’s sovereignty index praised Russia while criticizing Western countries and institutions, including the US, France, Germany and the EU. OpenAI also found that one operator generated German-language posts criticizing Ukraine, the EU and the German government while advocating closer ties with Russia. Another operator used the company’s tools to create logos for about a dozen Telegram channels focused on Germany, the US, France, Poland and Türkiye. The operation had limited immediate impact, with most social media posts receiving few views and the IBI’s official accounts attracting small audiences, OpenAI said. Some associated Telegram channels, however, had between 10,000 and 20,000 subscribers. The company said the operation was notable for building an apparently credible institutional structure that could be expanded over time to manufacture authority, obscure the origins of narratives and influence wider audiences. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Polish president visits Turkish defense industry stands at MSPO 2026 Türkiye accelerates digital infrastructure goals by hosting major tech event GITEX Ai Trump says Iran 'punished greatly' by US blockade Bosnia and Herzegovina expels 2 Serbian diplomats, withdraws support for regional cooperation declaration US sanctions 36 Iran-linked targets under ‘Economic D-Day’ campaign Kane, Mbappe headline 30-man shortlist for 2026 Ballon d’Or South African economy contracts 0.2% in second quarter, ending 6-quarter growth streak See All Russia rejects French cyberattack allegations, accuses Paris of reviving ‘Russian threat’ narrative Slovak police foil planned arson attack on drone factory, charge 3 foreigners

https://bnn-news.com/estonia-rejects-eu-.text: Photo: JUICE/Unsplash Advertisement The EU updated its Energy Efficiency Directive two and a half years ago, with one of its goals being to promote the widespread use of electric vehicles. For instance, a requirement is set to take effect next year mandating one EV charging station for every ten parking spaces at large non-residential buildings. Additionally, every second parking space must be equipped with the necessary connections to allow for the future installation of a charging station. Nele Peil, head of the Estonian Traders Association, stated a year and a half ago that the infrastructure investments required to meet the directive's minimum standards would cost companies between 500 million and 2 billion euros. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also remarked at the time that installing such connections in parking lots was not sensible and that the requirements needed to be discussed with the European Commission. The Estonian Ministry of Climate has decided not to implement this specific provision of EU legislation; consequently, it was omitted from the draft bill sent to stakeholders for review on Monday. Ivo Jaanisoo, Deputy Secretary General at the Ministry of Climate, stated that Estonia has proposed to the European Commission that requirements regarding charging stations for large parking lots be relaxed. He explained that, following consultations with business associations and an assessment of technological advancements since the directive's adoption, it is currently unclear how the new regulation could be implemented in Estonia in its present form. He emphasized that, for the promotion of sustainable transport, ensuring sufficient grid capacity to support existing practices is far more important. Advertisement Jaanisoo noted that all Member States are currently behind schedule in implementing the EU directive, and Estonia hopes that other nations will also reject the implementation of the requirements concerning charging infrastructure. However, these remain mere hopes for now, as the extent to which other countries will implement the directive's requirements is unknown. Discussions with other nations suggest that the issue is not a priority or a pressing concern elsewhere. Many countries have already made significant strides in developing electric vehicle charging infrastructure and possess large numbers of electric vehicles. Peil stated that the Estonian Traders Association supports the Ministry of Climate's plan, noting that some companies have likely already begun actively working to meet the directive's requirements—for instance, by establishing the necessary connections for charging stations. She pointed out that these companies would benefit even if the requirement were to be scrapped. She argued that, when choosing between making investments for 100% of parking spaces and bearing the full cost, versus addressing 20% ​​now and avoiding additional costs for the remaining 80%, the latter remains the better overall alternative to a 100% investment. According to data from the Estonian Transport Administration, there are currently nearly 12,300 electric vehicles in Estonia, representing less than 2% of the total vehicle fleet. The Ministry of Climate will accept feedback from stakeholders regarding the planned changes until the 28th of September. Photograph: Nine News/AAP View image in fullscreen NSW police say nine people were injured in the incident, prompting a major response from emergency services with four helicopters and 15 ambulances on scene. Photograph: Nine News/AAP Newcastle and the Hunter Several people injured after vehicle hits crowd in Newcastle waiting to farewell Knights team bus Driver arrested at the scene after a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Nino Bucci Fri 2 Oct 2026 22.48 EDT First published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ten people have been injured, two critically, after a car crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle waiting to farewell the Knights team bus before the NRL grand final. New South Wales police said a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man were in a critical condition, with eight others in a stable condition after the crash on Saturday morning. Those in a stable condition included a two-year-old girl and another five-year-old girl. The injured were treated on the scene by NSW ambulance paramedics, before being taken to John Hunter hospital. The P-plate driver was an 18-year-old man who was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory testing, police said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd. “Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said. “Police have commenced an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, with initial inquiries indicating it is not believed to be terror related.” Gavin Morris, the mayor of Newcastle, told the ABC that the driver, who he said was a Knights fan, lost control while revving his car shortly before the team arrived. “I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Morris said. “It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.” Footage posted on social media appeared to show the car being driven quickly around a roundabout shortly before the crash. Other images showed it had careened on to a footpath soon afterwards. A witness to the incident, Dylan Prior told ABC News that the car was “revving a bit” before it ran into a group of people. “I saw some young kids go flying, and people running to help the victims,” he said. “Everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver. “They were screaming for help.” The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession. The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Police appealed for fans to leave the area. “Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support. “Members of the public are asked to safely disperse from the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts. “Police thank the community for their patience, cooperation and assistance.” The NSW premier, Chris Minns, said his thoughts were with the families and friends of those injured. “It’s heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident,” he said. “We’ve seen how this grand final has brought Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.” The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had spoken with Minns and offered the federal government’s support. “My thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle,” Albanese said in a statement. “I want to acknowledge and thank emergency services and police for responding so quickly, and their ongoing work in treating the injured. “Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans.” NSW ambulance service has also been contacted for comment. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – The European Union is moving to unblock 4.2 billion euros ($4.8 billion) in funding for Hungary, saying the country’s new government has strengthened the rule of law, despite controversy over the president’s choice for chief prosecutor. Brussels proposed Wednesday releasing the financing from EU cohesion funds frozen during the 16-year rule of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Hungarian students and researchers are also set to regain access to EU educational and research programs, including the flagship Erasmus+ exchange and Horizon Europe programs. Get news worthy of your attention — delivered directly to your inbox. Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who ousted Orbán in a landslide election in April, had pledged during his campaign to secure billions of euros in EU funding blocked over corruption and rule-of-law concerns. His government has introduced changes aimed at strengthening judicial independence, making public procurement more transparent, reforming university governance, and strengthening oversight of how EU funds are spent. REFORMS UNLOCK FUNDS “Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union’s financial interests,” said Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm. “This shows that reforms deliver results,” she added. The latest measures follow the unlocking of about 10 billion euros ($11.4 billion) in COVID-19 pandemic recovery funding over the summer. Budapest expects the money to begin arriving later this year, subject to validation of reforms and submitted projects. If EU member states approve the Commission’s latest recommendation, Hungary will have unlocked most of the nearly 17 billion euros ($19.4 billion) in funding that had been blocked during the Orbán era. However, about 2.2 billion euros ($2.5 billion) remains frozen due to concerns about academic freedom, while another 500 million euros ($571 million) is blocked pending changes to Hungary’s controversial child-protection legislation. Hungary is also paying a daily 1 million euro ($1.14 million) fine after the EU’s top court ruled that Budapest had failed to comply with European asylum rules. PROSECUTOR DISPUTE Additionally, Magyar’s governing Tisza Party is clashing with newly installed President András Baka over the choice of Hungary’s next chief prosecutor, a key appointment in the government’s anti-corruption drive. Tisza lawmakers unanimously rejected Baka’s nomination of Zoltán Szathmáry, a senior career prosecutor. They asked the president to quickly nominate another candidate, Magyar announced on social media Tuesday. Baka, a former chief justice who took office last month with Tisza’s backing following the departure of his Orbán-allied predecessor, has so far stood by his nomination. The dispute highlights the importance of the chief prosecutor’s office as Magyar tries to tackle suspected high-level corruption and reduce the influence accumulated by Orbán and his allies during their years in power. Critics of the previous government, including anti-corruption organization Transparency International, have accused Orbán-era political loyalists in the prosecution service of contributing to a culture of impunity surrounding alleged high-level corruption. Orbán and senior prosecution officials have denied corruption and political favoritism in investigations. PROSECUTION SYSTEM Baka noted serious problems within the prosecution service. In an address to lawmakers Monday, he cautioned that an outsider could face major obstacles in reforming the institution. Tisza has not publicly detailed why its lawmakers rejected Szathmáry, but his senior role within the prosecution service during the Orbán era has fueled questions among government supporters about whether he represents the institutional change they expected after April’s election. The controversy comes as Magyar’s government seeks to show at home and in Brussels that it is reversing practices that fueled years of disputes with the EU. EU funding is crucial for Hungary’s strained finances, with the budget deficit expected to reach 7.5 percent of gross domestic product this year. Magyar’s government plans to reduce the deficit to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 as part of its longer-term ambition to meet the criteria for adopting the euro. EU RELATIONS RESET Hungary still faces unresolved disputes with Brussels, including over academic freedom, asylum policy and child-protection legislation. The government has signaled it wants to reach agreement with Brussels on the remaining issues by the end of the year as it seeks access to additional EU funds. Despite these issues, the Commission’s latest decision marks another significant step in rebuilding relations between Budapest and Brussels after years of confrontation during Orbán’s government. Von der Leyen had already highlighted Hungary’s changing direction in her State of the Union speech last week, telling lawmakers that years of “rule-of-law backsliding” were beginning to be reversed. Progress was being made in combating corruption and protecting fundamental rights, she noted. Yet the confrontation over the chief prosecutor suggests that Magyar’s effort to overhaul Hungary’s institutions will continue to generate political tensions, even as billions of euros in previously frozen EU funding move closer to Budapest.
